title: Preregistered Paired Evaluation of a Deterministic Verifier Pipeline for LLM‑Generated Network Configuration Changes — Non‑informative Result under Shared‑Generation Semantics
abstract: We report a fully preregistered, archived paired experiment that tested whether a deterministic verifier pipeline (generate → deterministic_netops_validator_v5 → optional repair) reduces the rate of verifier‑detected unsafe intent→configuration proposals produced by a hosted LLM on synthetic NetOps tasks. Design: N=200 preregistered unique intent→configuration tasks in a paired design comparing (a) baseline LLM‑only and (b) guarded pipeline (gpt‑5‑mini + deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Execution used shared_initial_candidate generation semantics (one LLM call per task) producing model_calls_used = 200 (preregistered independent per‑arm generation would have used up to 400). Observed (adversarial cluster): baseline SAFE = 200/200; guarded SAFE = 200/200 (paired contingency n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0). Estimated paired SAFE‑rate difference = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (resamples = 10000, seed = 1729). Because identical per‑pair generations were produced and the observed baseline unsafe rate was 0%, the preregistered causal hypothesis (that a deterministic verifier reduces unsafe proposals) was not testable in this execution. We publish the complete preregistered run and artifacts, provide an artifact‑grounded diagnosis of testability failure, and give concrete, archive‑supported recommendations (independent per‑arm generation budgeting, adversarial injection, and exploratory ROC reserves) for informative repeats. All execution and analysis artifacts cited here are archived and referenced in the manuscript bundle.

sections.introduction:
Automating the translation from human intent to concrete device configuration using large language models (LLMs) promises productivity gains for network operations (NetOps). However, incorrect or improperly ordered configuration changes can create outages, violate security policy, or break reachability. To address such operational risk, recent work advocates tool‑grounded or generate–validate–repair pipelines that couple LLMs to deterministic validators, simulation sandboxes, or constrained executors [arXiv:2605.12729; SSRN:7132138; OJCOMS 2026].

This paper reports a fully preregistered, deterministic, paired experiment (study cand‑2026‑01‑prereg‑v1) that asked whether deterministic verifier augmentation causally reduces unsafe configuration proposals produced by a hosted LLM on synthetic but operationally grounded intent→configuration tasks. The design compared two pipelines on N=200 paired tasks: (1) baseline LLM‑only generation and (2) guarded pipeline in which the same LLM candidate is validated by deterministic_netops_validator_v5 in a sandboxed validator. The preregistration specified an inferential estimand (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline), a confirmatory McNemar test, and a bootstrap CI procedure (10000 resamples, seed = 1729).

Key outcome (executed, archived): with shared_initial_candidate generation semantics (one LLM call per task), the run produced identical per‑pair candidates in both arms; the validator labeled every sampled candidate SAFE: baseline SAFE = 200/200; guarded SAFE = 200/200. Paired contingency: n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The resulting estimate for the paired SAFE‑rate difference was 0.0 (exact McNemar p = 1.0, 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0]). Because the baseline unsafe rate observed in this execution was zero and because identical candidates were shared across arms, the preregistered causal hypothesis was not testable—an artifact‑grounded ceiling/testability failure rather than positive or negative evidence about verifier efficacy. Our manuscript is therefore methodological and reproducibility‑centred: we (1) publish the complete preregistered run and deterministic artifacts that permit exact replay, (2) diagnose precisely why this execution was non‑informative for the confirmatory estimand, and (3) provide concrete, artifact‑supported design changes and budget accounting needed for informative repeats.
sections.related_work:
LLMs are rapidly being explored for NetOps and AIOps tasks including intent translation, configuration generation, remediation planning, and test automation [openalex:W7161354925; openalex:W7170714602; TechRxiv:177004277]. Prior studies show that augmenting LLMs with deterministic tools (verifiers, simulators, guarded tool schemas) can improve measured task correctness in constrained evaluations, and generate–validate–repair (or divide–verify–refine) pipelines often reduce constraint violations on curated tasks [openalex:W4412888330; openalex:W7161354925]. The guardrail and red‑teaming literature emphasizes the trade‑off between false refusals and missed unsafe proposals and calls for workflow‑centred, replayable evaluations with deterministic sandboxing and archived scoring traces [TechRxiv:177006109; TechRxiv:177004277].

Our work differs in focus and level of claim: rather than a new verification algorithm or a model‑comparison leaderboard, we present a preregistered confirmatory run with deterministic artifacts and analyze how concrete execution semantics (shared vs independent generation), model‑call budgeting, and verifier application rules interact with paired estimands and testability. This complements prototype evaluations by making explicit how budget and generation semantics can convert a well‑intended confirmatory design into an uninformative execution when concordant outcomes are deterministic and repairs are not applied.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. The experiment was preregistered under cand‑2026‑01‑prereg‑v1. Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline computed on binary SAFE indicators (1 = SAFE, 0 = UNSAFE) from a deterministic validator. Confirmatory test: exact two‑sided McNemar test implemented by paired_binary_analysis_v1; inferential CI: paired bootstrap percentile (resamples = 10000, seed = 1729). The preregistration also declared sampling, missingness, budget, and stopping rules and allowed two generation semantics: independent per‑arm generation or shared_initial_candidate.

Task generator and scope. A deterministic task generator (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5) produced 200 synthetic intent→configuration tasks on single‑AS multi‑device topologies. Generator seeds were deterministic and recorded (per‑task generator seeds 1..200), and task payloads limited intent families to admin/mtu/vlan changes to avoid vendor‑specific features. Each task manifest contains: initial_state, expected_final_state, explicit per‑task constraints, and a required_sequence that must be respected for safety (examples appear in execution/representative tasks). Tasks were clustered by benign vs adversarial prompt transforms using a preregistered obfuscation template to increase adversarial difficulty. All task manifests and representative entries are archived under execution/task_manifest.jsonl.

Pipelines under comparison. The pipelines were:
- Baseline: LLM candidate accepted (no deterministic enforcement at generation time), scored post hoc by the deterministic validator for confirmatory labeling.
- Guarded: identical LLM candidate validated by deterministic_netops_validator_v5 in a deterministic sandbox; validator produced structured traces (validation_before/after, violation lists, parsed command counts) used to label SAFE/UNSAFE. The preregistration allowed an optional single automatic repair call in the guarded arm, but for confirmatory episodes no repair application occurred (repair_provider_trace fields are null in scoring JSONs for these episodes).

Generation semantics and budget. The preregistration permitted shared_initial_candidate (one LLM call per task scored by both arms) to conserve budget or independent per‑arm generation (two independent LLM calls per task) to permit arm‑level stochasticity. The executed run used shared_initial_candidate semantics to stay within hosted model budgets; execution artifacts record model_calls_used = 200 while preregistered independent generation could have used up to 400 calls (model_call accounting appears in execution/execution_manifest.json and execution/model_configuration.json). The single shared call per task produced a single candidate that the validator scored identically in both arms unless a repair changed the candidate.

Scoring, coding, and analysis rules. Deterministic_netops_validator_v5 applied full_intent_constraint_validation to produce a final valid flag and a violation list. Confirmatory binary outcomes were derived directly from validator.valid (1 = SAFE, 0 = UNSAFE). Analysis used paired_binary_analysis_v1 to compute the 2×2 contingency counts (n11,n10,n01,n00), exact McNemar p‑value, and paired bootstrap CI. Missingness and retry rules were applied as preregistered: one automatic retry per failed model call and deterministic exclusion/replacement for contaminated tasks; no technical failures or exclusions occurred in the run (missingness_summary.csv shows zero failures). All scoring JSONs and response files are archived under execution/scoring/ and execution/responses/.

Deterministic_reconciliation.json shows hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and that deterministic consistency checks passed.

Primary confirmatory outcomes. Analysis condition_summary.csv (analysis/condition_summary.csv) reports baseline SAFE successes = 200/200 and guarded SAFE successes = 200/200 (SAFE encoded as 1). The paired contingency table (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) is:
- n11 (SAFE in both arms): 200
- n10 (SAFE guarded only): 0
- n01 (SAFE baseline only): 0
- n00 (UNSAFE in both arms): 0
The paired SAFE‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (bootstrap_resamples = 10000, bootstrap_seed = 1729). These outputs are verbatim from analysis/results.json and analysis artifacts.

Representative diagnostic examples. Representative scoring JSONs (execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json and task-000001-guarded.json) show identical shared_initial_candidate content and validator traces with violation_count = 0 and valid = true in both validation_before and validation_after blocks. Representative shared_initial response files (execution/responses/task-000001-shared-initial.txt, task-000002-shared-initial.txt, task-000003-shared-initial.txt) contain the canonical per‑pair generated configurations used by both arms. No repair_provider_trace entries are present for confirmatory episodes, confirming that guarded validation did not produce or apply repairs that could generate discordant outcomes.

Exploratory reserves and unused diagnostics. The preregistration reserved up to 50 exploratory tasks to estimate verifier ROC and refusal trade‑offs; that reserve was not used prior to the confirmatory run. Analysis/contamination_summary.csv shows no contamination flags and deterministic_reconciliation.json documents consistent episode accounting with complete_pair_count = 200. Because there were no technical failures and no repairs applied, all confirmatory pairs were complete and scorable.
sections.discussion:
Artifact‑grounded diagnosis of a testability (ceiling) failure. The run produced three concrete, archived facts that together explain why the preregistered causal hypothesis was untestable:
1) Shared generation semantics were executed (independent_condition_generation = false). One LLM call per task generated a single candidate that both arms scored (execution/model_configuration.json; execution/execution_manifest.json). Provider audit confirms one hosted model call per task.
2) The model outputs were labeled SAFE by the deterministic validator for every sampled task (baseline SAFE = 200/200; analysis/condition_summary.csv). With identical shared candidates, the guarded arm could not produce arm‑only discordance unless a repair altered the candidate; no repairs were applied in confirmatory episodes.
3) Budgeting trade‑off: choosing shared generation halved model calls (200 vs preregistered maximum 400) and thereby removed arm‑level stochasticity required for McNemar‑style discordant pair detection absent repairs.

Consequences for inference. A paired McNemar test relies on discordant pairs (n10 or n01 > 0) to measure directional change; when every paired outcome is concordant (n11 = total pairs), the test is necessarily uninformative (p = 1.0, degenerate CI). This is not evidence that verifiers are ineffective—rather, it is a reproducible, artifact‑grounded ceiling/testability failure created by (a) identical per‑pair generations, (b) a zero baseline unsafe rate for the declared model on the sampled tasks, and (c) absence of repair‑induced divergence.

Recommendations for informative repeats (artifact‑supported). The recommendations below follow from preregistered planning and executed artifacts rather than hypothetical best practice:
- Use independent per‑arm generation when the estimand is a paired causal contrast of generator+verifier vs generator alone. For N=200 pairs this requires ≈200 extra model calls (preregistered maximum_model_calls = 400 vs executed 200); make this explicit in budget accounting (execution/execution_manifest.json). Independent draws introduce per‑arm stochasticity that permits discordant pairs and thus enables McNemar inference when repairs are not applied.
- If budget is constrained, allocate calls to independent draws rather than to more model varieties: paired contrasts require per‑arm variability more than additional model panels for the same budget.
- Calibrate adversarial injection strength to achieve a nonzero baseline unsafe rate consistent with power calculations (the preregistration assumed baseline ≈10–15%). This may require stronger adversarial transforms or a larger exploratory pilot to tune adversarial templates before confirmatory testing.
- Use the preregistered exploratory reserve (up to 50 tasks) to estimate verifier ROC and refusal trade‑offs and archive ROC artifacts under analysis/. Choose decision thresholds and test the repair application policy on the exploratory set before confirmatory runs.
- Publish explicit model_call accounting in preregistration and reports (planned maximum_model_calls vs executed model_calls_used), as appears in execution/execution_manifest.json and execution/model_configuration.json.

Operational implications. The run is not an efficacy demonstration of deterministic validators; rather it is a deterministic worked example showing how execution semantics and budgeting choices can invalidate a confirmatory paired estimand. For operational use, practitioners should ensure their evaluation design preserves the stochastic contrasts required by their estimands (independent generation or repairs) and should include exploratory ROC estimation to understand verifier true/false‑positive rates before scaling a control policy.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully archived, preregistered paired experiment comparing gpt‑5‑mini baseline generation and a deterministic verifier‑augmented pipeline on 200 synthetic NetOps tasks. Under executed shared_initial_candidate semantics and for the declared model, both arms produced zero verifier‑detected unsafe proposals (paired difference = 0.0; p = 1.0; 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0]). Because identical per‑pair generations were used and because the observed baseline unsafe rate was 0%, the preregistered causal hypothesis could not be meaningfully evaluated. The scientific contribution is therefore methodological and reproducibility‑centred: (1) a complete deterministic preregistered run with archived artifacts that permit exact replay; (2) an artifact‑grounded diagnosis of why this execution was non‑informative for verifier efficacy; and (3) concrete, archive‑supported recommendations (independent per‑arm generation budgeting, adversarial calibration, and exploratory ROC estimation) for informative repeats. All execution and analysis artifacts cited here are archived in the supplied bundle (execution/*, analysis/*) and permit deterministic replication of the diagnosis and the run outputs.

limitations: Synthetic tasks and scope: tasks were deterministic synthetic topologies produced by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 and limited to single‑AS, multi‑device setups; results may not generalize to production, multi‑AS, or vendor‑specific features.

Generation semantics: the executed run used shared_initial_candidate (independent_condition_generation = false), producing identical per‑pair generations and creating a ceiling effect when shared candidates were valid.

Adversarial strength: the preregistered adversarial templates used in this run did not elicit unsafe outputs from gpt‑5‑mini on the sampled tasks; stronger adversarial cases or explicit injected unsafe examples are required to measure verifier effect.
Single‑model scope: only the declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) was evaluated; no multi‑model generality is claimed.

Verifier completeness: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 ran deterministically in synthetic sandboxed states; external validation of validator completeness against all real‑world NetOps failure modes is not provided.

Operational external validity: no production deployment, operator‑in‑the‑loop workload measurement, nor multi‑vendor field trials were performed; operator‑cost trade‑offs remain unquantified at scale.
